cards.explanation: Jacob says he wants to tell his sons “…what will happen to you in the days to come…” (Genesis 49:1). That's the whole agenda, friends. No small talk, no warm-up, just straight to the future. I'd be sitting up VERY straight in that room.

The answer is Reuben. Jacob says to him, “Reuben, you are my firstborn…” (Genesis 49:3). Firstborn means the oldest son, and Jacob calls him first. He also tells Reuben he is “…my might, and the beginning of my strength…”

The answer is False. After the praise, Jacob tells Reuben, “…you will no longer excel…” (Genesis 49:4). The reason he gives is that Reuben went up to his father's bed and defiled it. It's a heavy part of the blessing, and I think it hurts.

The answer is True. Jacob says, “May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly.” (Genesis 49:6). He's talking about Simeon and Levi. Council and assembly, and he wants no part of either one. This is one of the heavy parts of the blessing.

The answer is False. He doesn't keep them together. Jacob says of Simeon and Levi, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” (Genesis 49:7). Disperse and scatter both mean spreading out. It's a heavy part of the blessing.

The answer is that his brothers will praise him and bow down to him. Jacob says, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” and “your father’s sons shall bow down to you.” (Genesis 49:8). Praise AND bowing, friends. That's a double helping from his own brothers.

The answer is False. Jacob says nobody is poking this lion. He asks, “like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9). It's a question, and the answer is clearly no one. That's a lion you let sleep, friends.

The answer is that the allegiance of the nations is his. Jacob says the scepter stays with Judah “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.” (Genesis 49:10). Allegiance means loyalty, friends. So the loyalty of the nations is his. Jacob's words reach way past his own sons.

The answer is wine. Jacob says, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). Wine and the blood of grapes, friends. That picture is all about grapes. My laundry day has never looked like that.

The answer is that he bends his shoulder to the burden. Jacob says Issachar “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). Jacob first says he saw the resting place was good and the land pleasant. Then he picks up the load. I think that's a man who just gets to work.

The answer is False. The rider doesn't stay up there. Jacob says the viper “…bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.” (Genesis 49:17). Down he goes, backward. I would hate to be that rider.
The answer is the LORD. Jacob says, “I await Your salvation, O LORD.” (Genesis 49:18). He's speaking to the LORD in the middle of the blessings. It's a short line with a lot packed in.

The answer is that he attacks their heels. Jacob says, “Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels.” (Genesis 49:19). The raiders come first, and then Gad turns it around on them. That's a man who doesn't back down.

The answer is False. No dropping the bow here. Jacob says of Joseph, “Yet he steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). The archers attacked him and aimed at him, and he steadied his bow. Steadying it is the opposite of dropping it.

The answer is the Mighty One of Jacob. Think of a bow, friends. Jacob says Joseph “…steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). Then Jacob piles on more names: “…the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel…” I'd say Joseph didn't hold steady on his own power, because the Mighty One was holding him.

The answer is True. Jacob says, “May they rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the prince of his brothers.” (Genesis 49:26). Prince of his brothers, friends. That's a title Jacob gives him right to his face.
The answer is wolf. Jacob says, “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf…” (Genesis 49:27). Ravenous means hungry for it. Morning he eats, evening he shares. That's a full day's work.

The answer is False. The text says Jacob “…blessed each one with a suitable blessing.” (Genesis 49:28). Judah is pictured as a young lion, and Zebulun is told he will dwell by the seashore and become a harbor for ships. Different pictures for different sons.

The answers are fathers and Canaan. Jacob says, “Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite.” (Genesis 49:29). Fathers is his word, friends. He says Abraham and Sarah are buried in that cave, and Isaac and Rebekah too (Genesis 49:31). Jacob says the cave is “…in the field of Machpelah near Mamre, in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 49:30). That's where he wants to be buried, looking back to the land of his family.
The answer is Leah. Jacob says it himself: “…there I buried Leah.” (Genesis 49:31). He names Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah right before her. It's a family cave, and Leah's in it.
